It offered zero tax on income and profits, matching Singapore's competitiveness.
Its legal and regulatory framework sought to support international financial activity.

Consider the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), established in 2004. Instead of competing with established financial centers by offering lighter regulation, DIFC introduced English common law in the middle of a civil law country. DIFC created a parallel legal system with its own courts, judges, and precedents. International judges were recruited from the UK, Singapore, and Australia. Court proceedings were conducted in English. Judgments were based on common law principles.

The Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), established in 2004, created its own civil and commercial legal framework, with independent courts operating in English. Its statutes and court decisions govern DIFC law, supplemented by common-law principles consistent with those statutes. The courts may draw on decisions from England and Wales and other common-law jurisdictions.

This legal innovation solved a fundamental problem for international financial institutions. They understood common law, had contracts written for common law, and trusted common law courts. Operating under civil law, especially Middle Eastern civil law derived from Egyptian and French traditions, created uncertainty that no tax incentive could overcome. DIFC removed this uncertainty entirely. A contract signed in DIFC would be interpreted exactly as it would in London.

The framework gave international financial institutions access to a common-law court system and procedures they could assess. Contract disputes remain subject to the applicable governing law. DIFC's own statutes and judgments determine its law; the jurisdiction is distinct from England and Wales.
Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM), established in 2015, took this even further. ADGM directly applied English common law.
Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM), established in 2015, directly applies English common law, including equity, subject to local adaptations and overriding ADGM enactments or applicable Abu Dhabi law.

English court judgments were directly enforceable. English statutes applied until ADGM created its own. It adopted the legal system itself. For international businesses, ADGM was legally indistinguishable from operating in London, but with better weather and no taxes.

ADGM incorporates selected English statutes through its own legislation. Qualifying judgments from England and Wales's Commercial Court can be registered and enforced through ADGM's statutory procedures, subject to eligibility conditions and grounds for setting registration aside. Businesses gain access to an established body of commercial law within a distinct local jurisdiction.
The UAE opened its economy broadly to foreign investment, foreign ownership, and foreign workers across sectors.

Free zones opened routes for foreign investors and workers to participate in the UAE economy. Jafza allowed full foreign ownership of licensed free-zone companies without a UAE national shareholder. The scope of ownership rights remained subject to the applicable activity and legal regime.
